plan.curriculum: Mathematics 2.0, Statistics, Years 5 and 6 (VC2M5ST03, VC2M6ST03): plan statistical investigations by posing and refining questions, including survey questions that are objective and balanced
plan.shape: compare-two-models: an unfair survey question beside a fair one, because spotting what makes a question fair is the new idea
plan.criticalFeature: a fair survey question does not push people towards an answer, and every person has a choice that fits
decisionPoints: the choice check: which survey question is fair?
plan.anchor: ask, collect, show, tell: every investigation starts with a fair question and ends with what the data shows

studentTools: Printed Worksheet for every student; Extension and Supported Worksheet as needed
routineIcons: Write it, chin it, show me
boardSetup: The week's anchor on the board: ask, collect, show, tell
Two columns headed Fair and Unfair, for sorting questions during the I Do

resources.label: Worksheet
resources.description: Your turn. Sort statistical questions, categorical or numerical, fix unfair questions, and plan a canteen survey.
resources.title: Asking Fair Statistical Questions
resources.subtitle: A fair question does not push, and has a choice for everyone.

example.prompt: Is 'How many pets do our families have?' a statistical question?
steps: Ask: would different people give different answers?
Yes, families have different numbers of pets.
So we need to collect data.

items.prompt: Sort the questions. Do the answers vary, or is there only one answer?
cards: How many students walk to school?
How long do students read each night?

answers vary (statistical): How many students walk to school?
How long do students read each night?

items.prompt: Will the answers be categorical (words or groups) or numerical (numbers)? Write C or N.
rows: How many books did you read this term?
Which pet would you most like?
How many minutes do you read each night?
answers: How many books did you read this term?
Which pet would you most like?
How many minutes do you read each night?

example.prompt: Fix: 'Wouldn't a longer lunch be great?'
steps: Find the push: 'Wouldn't... be great' wants a yes.
Remove the push.
Give choices for everyone.
example.answer: How long should lunch be: 30, 40, 50 minutes or other?

items.prompt: Liam wrote this survey question. Find the problem and fix it.
work: Don't you love our new playground?
items.answer: It pushes people to say yes. Fair: What do you think of the new playground? love it / like it / not sure / do not like it.

items.prompt: Ava gave these choices. Find the problem and fix it.
work: How many hours of screen time each day?
items.answer: The choices overlap (1 and 2 are in two boxes) and miss more than 3. Fix: 0, 1, 2, 3, more than 3 hours.

example.prompt: The library wants to know which books to buy. Plan the question.
steps: Decide what you need to know: favourite type of book.
Write it without a push.
Give choices for everyone, including other.
example.answer: What type of book do you like most: adventure, funny, mystery, fact books or other?

items.prompt: The canteen wants to sell a new lunch. Write a fair survey question with choices for everyone. Say who you would ask, and whether the answers will be categorical or numerical.
items.answer: For example: Which new lunch would you most like: wraps, pasta, sushi, soup or other? Ask students from every year level. Categorical: the answers are foods.

resources.label: Extension
resources.description: Early finisher option. Who to ask, choices with no gaps or overlaps, and designing your own two-question survey, with worked examples.
resources.title: Extension: Survey Detectives
resources.subtitle: A fair survey asks fair questions of the right people.

example.prompt: To find the school's favourite sport, Sam asks only the netball team. Is that fair?
steps: Think about who was asked.
Netball players are more likely to choose netball.
Not fair: ask students from every class.

items.prompt: To find out how students get to school, Jade asks only the students in the bike shed. Is that fair? Explain.
items.answer: Not fair: everyone in the bike shed rides a bike. Ask students from all over the school.

items.prompt: To find the class's favourite fruit, Omar asks every student in the class. Is that fair? Explain.
items.answer: Fair: everyone in the class is asked, so every answer counts.

example.prompt: Fix the choices 0 to 5, 5 to 10 pets.
steps: 5 is in two boxes: an overlap.
More than 10 has no box: a gap.
0 to 4, 5 to 9, 10 or more.

items.prompt: Each set of choices has a problem. Name it and write a fixed set.

example.prompt: Design two questions about weekend sport.
steps: One categorical: Which sport do you play most?
One numerical: How many hours of sport do you play?
Check both are fair.

items.prompt: Design a two-question survey about a topic you choose: one categorical question and one numerical question. Give fair choices for both.
items.answer: Check: one question has word answers, one has number answers; no pushing words; choices have no gaps or overlaps and include everyone.

resources.label: Supported Worksheet
resources.description: For students who need more guidance: pushing words to circle, one missing choice at a time, and a hint on every question.
resources.title: Fair Questions: Step by Step
resources.subtitle: Look for the push. Check the choices.

example.prompt: Circle the pushing words: 'Isn't maths the best subject?'
steps: Read it aloud.
'Isn't... the best' wants you to say yes.
Circle 'Isn't' and 'the best'.

items.prompt: Circle the pushing words: 'Don't you agree dogs are better than cats?'
items.hint: Which words want you to say yes?

items.prompt: Circle the pushing words: 'Surely homework is boring?'

example.prompt: 'What is your favourite pet? dog / cat' needs another choice.
steps: Some people like fish or birds.
Add 'other' so everyone can answer.

items.prompt: 'Which season do you like best? summer / winter' Add the missing choices.
'How do you get to school? walk / car' Add choices so everyone fits.

example.prompt: 'How many brothers do you have?' C or N?
steps: The answers are numbers: 0, 1, 2...
Numbers mean numerical.

items.prompt: 'What is your favourite colour?' C or N?
items.hint: Are the answers words or numbers?

items.prompt: 'How many minutes do you walk each day?' C or N?
items.hint: Are the answers words or numbers?

slides.notes: Session 1 of our statistics week: today we learn to ask fair questions.
Before you start, put boards and markers on every desk. Print the Worksheet for everyone, and a few copies of the Extension and the Supported Worksheet.

slides.title: Read a point
prompts: What are the coordinates of B?

beats: SAY: Let's warm up with last week's coordinates.
ASK: What are the coordinates of B?
15 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: (6, 2)
SCAN boards, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal and move straight on.
Less -> slide across, then up, together on the big grid. Re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: It's 6, 2. Across first, then up. Tick it or fix it.
trap: writing (2, 6).
Fix: say the anchor, across the corridor, then up the stairs, and they rewrite it.
notes.prep: Review of Week 2 coordinates (the request named the focus). Keep the review under 6 minutes.

beats: ASK: Which quadrant is the point negative 3, 4 in?
15 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: the second
SCAN boards, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal and move straight on.
Less -> say left or right, then up or down,
and trace it on the four-quadrant grid. Re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: It's the second quadrant: 3 left and 4 up. Tick it or fix it.
trap: saying the third.
Fix: ask whether 4 is up or down, and they rename it.

beats: ASK: How big is angle x?
20 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 37
SCAN boards, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, then on to Fluency.
Less -> trace the straight line, say 180, then subtract. Re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: It's 37 degrees, because 180 take away 143 is 37.
Tick it or fix it.
trap: writing 53, from 90.
Fix: trace the straight line, and they redo it from 180.
notes.prep: Week 1 review: angles on a straight line.

slides.title: Subtract with the written method: 3 digits

beats: SAY: Now for some written subtraction.
Line up the places, and always start with the ones.
ASK: Use the written method to solve this one.
30 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 344
SCAN boards for the regrouped columns.
80%+ -> reveal, then the next one.
Less -> model the first column together on the board, re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: The answer is 344.
Tick it or fix it, and check every step.
trap: taking the smaller digit from the bigger one in every column.
Fix: ask "Is the top digit big enough?", and they regroup and redo it.
notes.prep: Subtraction fluency: 3 digits, then 4, then 5. Keep the whole block under 6 minutes.

slides.title: Subtract with the written method: 4 digits

beats: SAY: Now it's 4 digits.
It's the same method, just one more column.
ASK: Use the written method to solve this one.
45 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 3 255
SCAN boards for the regrouped columns.
80%+ -> reveal, then the next one.
Less -> model the first column together on the board, re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: The answer is 3 255.
Tick it or fix it, and check every step.
trap: taking the smaller digit from the bigger one in every column.
Fix: ask "Is the top digit big enough?", and they regroup and redo it.

slides.title: Subtract with the written method: 5 digits

beats: SAY: Now it's 5 digits.
It's the same method, just one more column.
ASK: Use the written method to solve this one.
60 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 22 358
SCAN boards for the regrouped columns.
80%+ -> reveal, then the learning intention.
Less -> model the first column together on the board, re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: The answer is 22 358.
Tick it or fix it, and check every step.
trap: taking the smaller digit from the bigger one in every column.
Fix: ask "Is the top digit big enough?", and they regroup and redo it.

slides.learningIntention: We are learning to write fair questions for a statistical investigation.
successCriteria: I can tell whether a question needs data to answer it.
I can write a survey question that is fair and has a choice for everyone.
I can explain whether the answers will be categorical or numerical.

beats: POINT to the learning intention.
SAY: This week we're running our own statistical investigation.
It starts with asking a good question.
SAY: Let's read our I can statements together.
Cue: Everyone, together, on three.
SAY: The first one is where we start,
and the second one is our big goal today.
notes.prep: SC1 spotting a statistical question is reachable for everyone; SC2 writing a fair question is the core and the exit evidence; SC3 categorical and numerical is the stretch.

slides.title: Which question needs data?
lines: How tall is our classroom door?
How do students in our class get to school?

notes.answer: the second: answers vary from person to person
beats: POINT to each question.
SAY: Here are two questions.
One has a single answer,
and the other needs lots of answers from lots of people.
ASK: Which question needs us to collect data from lots of people?
Show one or two fingers.
10 sec. Cue: Fingers at your chest... show me.
EXPECT: two fingers
SCAN fingers.
80%+ -> cold call one student: Why does it need lots of answers?
Less -> ask: if I asked five people about the door,
would their answers differ? Re-ask.
SAY: The second one is a statistical question, because the answers vary.
Today we'll learn to ask questions like that fairly.
trap: choosing the door question.
Fix: ask whether everyone would give a different answer, and they choose again.
notes.prep: The launch comes after the LI: a statistical question has answers that vary. Under 4 minutes.

slides.meaning: When a question or survey pushes people towards one answer.
slides.example: "Don't you agree footy is the best?" has bias.

beats: POINT to the word.
SAY: This word is bias. Say it with me: bi-as.
SAY: A question has bias when it pushes people towards one answer.
The scales are tipped before anyone answers.
ASK: Does 'What is your favourite sport?' have bias?
Thumbs up for yes, down for no.
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: thumbs down
trap: thinking any question about a favourite is biased.
Fix: ask which words push, and they check again.
notes.prep: Bias is today's key idea; unfair and pushing are fine in speech.

slides.title: Spot the push
steps: Read the question aloud.
Find the pushing words: Don't you agree, the best.
Take them out.
Ask it fairly.

visual.text: Don't you agree that footy is the best sport?

beats: POINT to the question.
SAY: Let me read this survey question aloud and listen for a push.
MODEL underlining the pushing words.
SAY: 'Don't you agree' wants me to say yes,
and 'the best' tells me the answer.
That's bias, so the data wouldn't be fair.
ASK: How could we ask this fairly?
20 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: What is your favourite sport?
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: What is your favourite sport? Now it doesn't push,
so every answer is a real answer.
trap: keeping 'the best' in the new question.
Fix: read it aloud and listen for the push, and they rewrite it.
notes.stretch: Write a biased question about lunch, then fix it.
notes.help: Cover the pushing words with your finger and read what is left.
notes.prep: A fair question has no pushing words. SC2.

slides.title: A choice for everyone
steps: Read the choices.
Ask: can every person tick a box?
Someone who plays 10 hours has no box.
Add: more than 8 hours.

rows: How many hours of sport do you play each week?

notes.answer: more than 8 hours has no box
beats: POINT to the choices.
SAY: This question doesn't push, but let's check the choices too.
MODEL testing two people.
SAY: If I play 1 hour, I tick the first box.
But what if I play 10 hours?
ASK: Who can't tick a box, and how would you fix it?
20 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: someone who plays more than 8 hours: add 'more than 8'
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: Someone who plays more than 8 hours has no box,
so we add 'more than 8 hours'.
trap: adding a box that overlaps, like 8 to 10.
Fix: ask where someone who plays 8 hours ticks, and they fix it.
notes.help: Test the choices with made-up people.
notes.prep: A fair question gives every person a choice that fits. SC2.

slides.title: Two kinds of data
lines: Categorical: words or groups, like favourite sport.
Numerical: numbers you count or measure, like hours of sport.

beats: SAY: Data comes in two kinds.
Categorical data is words or groups, like which sport you like best.
SAY: Numerical data is numbers we count or measure,
like how many hours of sport you play.
ASK: Is 'How many pets do you have?' categorical or numerical?
10 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: numerical
trap: calling it categorical because pets are things.
Fix: ask whether the answers are words or numbers, and they rename it.
notes.stretch: Think of a question that could be asked both ways.
notes.help: Ask: are the answers words, or numbers?
notes.prep: Naming the kind of data now sets up choosing a graph in Session 3. SC3.

slides.title: Which survey question is fair?
slides.prompt: Point to A, B or C

options.text: Don't you agree recess should be longer?
How long should recess be: 15, 20, 25, 30 minutes or other?
Is recess too short, or way too short?
options.misconception: accepts choices that all lean one way

beats: SAY: Read each question to yourself.
Check for a push, and check the choices.
ASK: Which survey question is fair?
20 sec. Cue: Voices off. Point... now. Hold your point.
EXPECT: pointing to B
SCAN the room, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, then cold call one student: What is unfair about C?
Less -> read each one aloud and underline any push together. Re-ask.
REVEAL after pointing is scanned.
SAY: It's B. It doesn't push,
and its choices fit everyone, including 'other'.
trap: pointing to C.
Fix: ask what you tick if recess is just right, and they choose again.
notes.prep: First decision point. A means pushing words are missed; C means one-sided choices are missed.

slides.title: Categorical or numerical?
slides.ask: Will the answers be categorical or numerical? Write C or N.
slides.pivot: ask: are the answers words or numbers?
slides.followUp: cold call one board: How do you know?

items.text: How many siblings do you have?
How far do you live from school?
Which day of the week were you born?
What size shoe do you wear?
items.say: Numerical. Shoe sizes are measurements, even though we say them as names.

say: Write C or N on your board for each question.
trap: calling 'which day' numerical because days have dates.
Fix: ask whether the answers are words or numbers, and they redo it.
notes.stretch: Rewrite one categorical question so it collects numbers instead.
notes.help: Say one possible answer out loud first, then decide.
notes.prep: Guided practice with a tricky edge case at the end. SC3.

slides.title: What needs fixing?
slides.prompt: How do you get to school? walk / car

options.text: It pushes people to one answer.
options.misconception: confuses missing choices with a pushing question

options.text: Some people have no choice that fits.

options.misconception: only checks for pushing words, not the choices

notes.answer: B: some people have no choice
beats: SAY: This one is just for you.
Read the question and the choices carefully.
ASK: What needs fixing in this survey question?
15 sec. Cue: Voices off. Point... now. Hold your point.
EXPECT: pointing to B
SCAN every point, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, then Your turn.
Less -> test it with three people:
one who walks, one by bus, one by bike. Re-ask.
REVEAL after pointing is scanned.
SAY: It's B. Anyone who catches a bus or rides a bike has no box,
so we add bus, bike and other.
trap: pointing to C.
Fix: ask where a bike rider ticks, and they choose again.
notes.prep: The hinge before independent work. Anyone choosing C starts on the Supported Worksheet with the teacher.

slides.title: Your turn
slides.task: Sort, fix and write fair questions on your worksheet.

beats: POINT to the steps.
SAY: Read each question carefully, solve it carefully, then check your answers.
SAY: If you finish, the Extension is your early finisher option.
Let's read the steps together. Cue: Everyone, together, on three.
CIRCULATE and ask: Does your question push? Is there a box for everyone?
TIME: 20 minutes. Stop everyone once at 10 minutes to share a strategy.
trap: writing a fair question with too few choices.
Fix: test the choices with three made-up people, and they add one.
notes.stretch: Extension: who to ask, choices with no gaps or overlaps, and designing your own survey.
notes.help: Supported Worksheet: pushing words to circle, one missing choice at a time, and hints.
notes.prep: Independent practice: statistical or not, C or N, fixing questions and planning a survey. The sheet is evidence for SC2 and SC3.

slides.title: Show what you know
questions: Write a fair survey question about favourite school subjects. Give choices for everyone.

notes.answer: a question with no push, several subjects, and 'other'
beats: SAY: Here's the last one. Work it out on your own board.
ASK: Write a fair survey question about favourite school subjects, with choices for everyone.
60 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: a question with no push, several subjects, and 'other'
RECORD who writes a push or leaves people without a choice.
They start tomorrow's survey with the teacher.
trap: writing 'Isn't maths the best?'
Fix: none now. Record the name for tomorrow.
notes.prep: Exit evidence for SC2: a new topic, written from scratch.

slides.reflectionPrompt: Tell your partner the two checks for a fair question.

notes.answer: open - listen for no push, and a choice for everyone
beats: SAY: Let's read our I can statements together.
Cue: Everyone, together, on three.
ASK: How sure are you that you can write a fair survey question?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: thumbs up, sideways or down
RECORD each thumb down beside the exit board.
A thumb up with a pushing question on the board matters most.
ASK: What are the two checks for a fair question?
20 sec. Cue: Partner A first. You have 20 seconds. Go.
EXPECT: no push, and a choice for everyone
notes.prep: Read the self-assessment beside the exit evidence. Tomorrow we run our survey.
